title: An implanted interface restored communication at home for nearly seven years
summary: A woman with locked-in ALS used the Utrecht NeuroProsthesis to communicate at home for nearly seven years.
account: A woman with locked-in ALS received the Utrecht NeuroProsthesis in October 2015. After training, she selected letters and called a caregiver by attempting to move her hand. Caregivers set up the equipment, but she then used it without research staff. It became her only technological means of communication after she lost reliable eye tracking. Home use continued for nearly seven years and ended in March 2023 as control became unreliable. Researchers considered ALS-related brain changes the likely explanation, without proving a single cause. The documented decoder combined brain-signal features and fitted thresholds rather than a named machine-learning model.
purpose: Provide autonomous communication for a person with late-stage ALS who could no longer rely on eye tracking
system: Utrecht NeuroProsthesis with Medtronic Activa PC+S and Tobii Communicator 5
developer: University Medical Center Utrecht (Brain Center; Ramsey and Vansteensel)
deployer: University Medical Center Utrecht; home use by the participant
segment: People with locked-in syndrome from ALS

ratings.reason: The participant regained a lasting ability to communicate at home. The reports do not establish prevention of a separate serious harm.

ai_role.statement: The documented decoder combines normalized brain-signal features and fitted thresholds to generate clicks. Whether that mechanism qualifies as AI remains unresolved. The communication benefit itself is documented.
